```{r setup}
library(blockr.ui)
```

The package blockr.ui is the UI kit of blockr's client, the part of blockr that runs in the browser.
Every UI that a blockr package draws there takes its look from blockr.ui.
That holds for core's UIs, for the frontend that draws the page, such as the dock, and for the UIs of blocks and plugins.
They draw with the components of blockr.ui.
The colours, faces, sizes, corners and shadows that they draw come from blockr.ui's theme variables, but for the few exceptions that [Colours](#colours) names.
So a frontend restyles every UI on the page by setting theme variables, and so does an app.

This article is for the authors of those UIs and of frontends.
It covers four things:

1. The theme variables: what each is for, its defaults, how a frontend gives values of its own, and how the frontend's tests list the defaults that it keeps.
2. The components: what blockr.ui offers, its icons, how an input takes its value through `bound`, and how a package tests what it draws.
3. How a package builds against blockr.ui: the build preset, the package's prefix, and the list of theme variables with its checks.
4. How an app gives the page a theme of its own.

## The theme variables

The theme variables are the CSS variables that give the page its look.
Each has a job, which says what it is for, such as the colour of a menu.
Each has a name under the prefix `bk`, such as `--bk-color-popover`.
Every UI draws with them, so a value that a theme sets reaches every UI at once.
A theme is values for some of the theme variables, in light mode and in dark mode.

The function `theme_variables()` lists them:

```{r}
theme_variables()
```

The list holds the colours, the two faces, four sizes of text, the radius, three shadows, the spacing and the layer of the overlays.
It holds only what a frontend may want to set for its own look.
The rest of how a component looks, such as the weight of its text or the timing of its transitions, belongs to the component.

The classes in this section are written without a prefix, as `bg-warning/10`.
A package writes each class under a prefix of its own, as core writes `bc:bg-warning/10` ([Prefixes](#prefixes)).

### Colours

The colours take the names that [shadcn/ui](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/theming) gives their jobs, so authors of UIs on Tailwind CSS know them already.
In these names, the text of the page is `foreground` and the brand colour is `primary`.
The name `accent` means the fill of a hovered row, not the brand colour.
A UI takes each colour by its job:

| Variables | Job |
|---|---|
| `--bk-color-background`, `--bk-color-foreground` | The page, which the frontend draws behind its panels and cards, and the text on it |
| `--bk-color-card`, `--bk-color-card-foreground` | A card or a node on the page or in a panel, such as a block's card in the dock or a node of the DAG, and its text. The colour is opaque, since a node covers the links below it |
| `--bk-color-popover`, `--bk-color-popover-foreground` | Every overlay, such as a menu, a select's list, a popover, a dialog, a tooltip or a toast, and its text. The colour is opaque, since an overlay covers the page |
| `--bk-color-primary`, `--bk-color-primary-foreground`, `--bk-color-primary-text` | The brand colour, for what is picked, checked, selected or current, and for the primary button; the text and icons on it; and the text of a link or of a message |
| `--bk-color-secondary`, `--bk-color-secondary-foreground` | A filled control of lower emphasis, and its text. No component of blockr.ui fills with it yet |
| `--bk-color-muted`, `--bk-color-muted-foreground` | A quiet fill inside a surface, such as a tag or a block of code, and secondary text, such as a hint, a placeholder or a count |
| `--bk-color-accent`, `--bk-color-accent-foreground` | A row or a button that is hovered, pressed or focused from the keyboard, and its text |
| `--bk-color-destructive`, `--bk-color-destructive-foreground`, `--bk-color-destructive-text` | An error, and what removes something, such as the destructive button; the text on a fill of it; and the text of an error |
| `--bk-color-warning`, `--bk-color-warning-foreground`, `--bk-color-warning-text` | A warning; the text on a fill of it; and the text of a warning |
| `--bk-color-success`, `--bk-color-success-foreground`, `--bk-color-success-text` | A success, such as the status dot of a block that is `ready`; the text on a fill of it; and the text of a success |
| `--bk-color-border` | Outlines and dividers, such as the edge of a card or an overlay, the rules of a table and a menu's divider |
| `--bk-color-input` | The edge of a field, and the outline of a checkbox, a radio button, a switch or a drop zone |
| `--bk-color-ring` | The focus ring |

Each of the four colours `primary`, `destructive`, `warning` and `success` comes with three variables:

1. The colour itself draws a mark, an edge or a fill.
   It also draws the tints of a banner, a pill or a toast, through Tailwind's opacity modifier, as `bg-warning/10`.
2. Its `-foreground` draws text on a fill of the colour, as on the destructive button.
3. Its `-text` draws text in the colour, on any surface and on the colour's own tint, as an error's message does.

One colour cannot do all three jobs in both modes.
White text reaches a contrast of 4.8:1 on the red of the destructive button in light mode.
On the lighter red of dark mode, it reaches only 2.8:1.
So the destructive button's text takes the variable `--bk-color-destructive-foreground`, whose default in dark mode is nearly black.

The variable `--bk-color-input` stands out more than `--bk-color-border`.
A field's edge alone marks the field, while a border only divides.
In the same way, the outline alone marks a checkbox that is not checked.

The hover, `accent`, differs from the quiet fill, `muted`, so that a hovered row stands out on a menu.
Secondary text in `muted-foreground` reaches less than the contrast of 4.5:1 that text needs on `accent`.
So a hovered row draws its secondary text in `accent-foreground` too.

Two parts of the components take plain black or white rather than a theme variable, since each must stand out on any colour.
One is the backdrop behind a modal, black at 40%, which dims whatever page lies below it.
The other is the black and white rings around a colour field's thumbs and swatches, which show on any colour that the user picks.

The theme variables hold no other colour.
The build preset drops Tailwind's palette.
So a class such as `bg-blue-600` writes nothing, and the check of the preset fails it ([The checks](#the-checks)).
A UI that needs a shade between two variables mixes them in its stylesheet, as `color-mix(in oklab, var(--bk-color-primary) 15%, var(--bk-color-card))`.
It may also tint one variable with the opacity modifier, as `bg-primary/20`.
Both follow the theme and the mode.
A UI writes a colour that must stay fixed on purpose, as the arbitrary value `bg-[#0072b2]`.
The colours of data, such as the series of a chart, do not come from the theme variables.
A package that draws data takes them from elsewhere, such as the palettes of blockr.theme.

The theme variables hold no colour for the status of a block or for the category of a block class, since both are core's.
Core draws each status in the colour of a job, as it draws the status dot of a `ready` block in `success`.
Core keeps the colours of the categories outside every theme.
An app sets them through core's blockr option `category_colors`.
Where blockr's packages need a colour that no variable gives, a later version of blockr.ui adds it to the theme variables, as it added `warning` and `success` to the colours of shadcn/ui.

### Fonts, sizes, radii, shadows and spacing

The other theme variables take the names of Tailwind's theme:

| Variables | Job |
|---|---|
| `--bk-font-sans`, `--bk-font-mono` | The face of every UI's text, and of its code |
| `--bk-text-xs`, `--bk-text-sm`, `--bk-text-base`, `--bk-text-lg` | The four sizes of text, from a hint's up to a dialog's title. The line height of each size follows the size |
| `--bk-radius` | The base of every corner |
| `--bk-shadow-sm`, `--bk-shadow-md`, `--bk-shadow-lg` | The shadow of a thumb, such as a slider's; of what floats over the page, such as a menu or a tooltip; and of a dialog or a sheet |
| `--bk-spacing` | The unit of every padding, margin, gap and size of a component, as `px-2` pads by twice it |
| `--bk-z-index-overlay` | The layer that every overlay stacks on, above everything else on the page |

Every corner derives from `--bk-radius`.
The class `rounded-lg` draws the radius itself, and each other step is a multiple of it, from 0.6 of it for `rounded-sm` to 2.6 of it for `rounded-4xl`.
So a theme sets one value, and every corner follows.
A pill stays round under every theme, since `rounded-full` reads no variable.

Each of these scales has fewer steps than Tailwind's.
A class of a step that the theme variables lack, such as `shadow-2xl` or `text-xl`, writes nothing, and the check fails it.
A UI draws the nearest step that the scale holds instead.

The sizes of text and the spacing are theme variables too.
So a frontend sets the type and the density of every UI.
A component takes each of its sizes from them, so that the frontend's values reach it.
A field's height, for one, is a multiple of the spacing.

### The defaults

The stylesheet of blockr.ui gives every theme variable a default, in light mode and in dark mode.
The defaults roughly keep the look of blockr.ui 0.0.1.
Each default is a fixed value.
No default comes from what surrounds an element on the page.
A page draws in the defaults wherever neither its frontend nor the app sets a value.

This table shows the defaults as the stylesheet of the installed blockr.ui sets them:

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
# The stylesheet of blockr.ui, as its build writes it.
css <- trimws(
  readLines(system.file("js", "blockr-ui.css", package = "blockr.ui"))
)

# The theme variables that a rule of the stylesheet sets, with their values,
# named by the variables.
rule_values <- function(selector) {
  from <- match(paste(selector, "{"), css)
  to <- from + match("}", css[-seq_len(from)])
  lines <- css[seq(from + 1L, to - 1L)]
  lines <- sub(";$", "", lines[startsWith(lines, "--bk-")])
  structure(sub("^[^:]+:\\s*", "", lines), names = sub(":.*$", "", lines))
}

both <- rule_values(":root")

defaults <- list(
  light = c(both, rule_values(":root[data-bk-mode=\"light\"]")),
  dark = c(both, rule_values(":root[data-bk-mode=\"dark\"]"))
)

vars <- theme_variables()

stopifnot(
  all(vars %in% names(defaults$light)),
  all(vars %in% names(defaults$dark))
)

# A value as the table shows it, after a swatch for a colour.
shown <- function(value, var) {
  swatch <- ifelse(
    startsWith(var, "--bk-color-"),
    paste0(
      "<span style=\"display: inline-block; width: 1em; height: 1em; ",
      "vertical-align: -0.15em; border: 1px solid #888; ",
      "border-radius: 2px; background: ", value, ";\"></span> "
    ),
    ""
  )
  paste0(swatch, "`", value, "`")
}

cat(
  "| Variable | Light mode | Dark mode |",
  "|---|---|---|",
  paste0(
    "| `", vars, "` | ", shown(defaults$light[vars], vars),
    " | ", shown(defaults$dark[vars], vars), " |"
  ),
  sep = "\n"
)
```

In dark mode, `popover` is lighter than `card`, so a menu stands apart from the card that it opens from.
In light mode, both are white, and a menu stands apart by its border and its shadow.
The sans face is Open Sans.
Its files ship with blockr.ui, and blockr.ui's stylesheet writes its faces.

### Light mode and dark mode

Every theme gives each variable that it sets a value for light mode and one for dark mode.
So no theme is light or dark alone.
Core's board option `dark_mode` switches the page between the two modes.
It sets the attribute `data-bk-mode` on the page's root to `light` or `dark`.
The value of `dark_mode` stays with the user, in the browser, rather than with the board.

The page knows its mode before it first paints:

1. R writes into the page's head a line of JavaScript, which runs as the page loads.
2. The line reads the user's pick of `dark_mode` from the browser's storage.
   Where the user has picked nothing, it takes the blockr option `dark_mode`.
   Where that is not set either, it takes the mode that the user's system prefers.
3. The line sets `data-bk-mode` before the page first paints.
4. Once the board opens, the board option `dark_mode` reads the same three values.
   It switches the attribute whenever the user picks the other mode.

Every job has a value in both modes, so a UI that draws with the jobs needs no `dark:` variant.
The variant, as in `dark:bg-card`, applies where `data-bk-mode` is `dark`.
It serves only what a package draws beyond the jobs.

### A frontend's values

A frontend sets the theme variables whose values it wants its own, and keeps blockr.ui's defaults for the rest.
It gives its values as a theme, which `new_blockr_theme()` makes.
Its method of core's generic `frontend_theme()` returns that theme.
Core's `serve()` calls `frontend_theme()` on the app's frontend as it builds the app.
Say a frontend draws grey menus, and sets its controls closer together than blockr.ui does.
Its method might be this:

```r
frontend_theme.my_frontend <- function(x, ...) {
  new_blockr_theme(
    light = list("--bk-color-popover" = "#fafafa", "--bk-spacing" = "0.22rem"),
    dark = list("--bk-color-popover" = "#262626", "--bk-spacing" = "0.22rem")
  )
}
```

Each value of `light` holds in light mode alone, and each value of `dark` in dark mode alone.
So the frontend gives the spacing, which it wants in both modes, in both lists.
Core writes the theme into the page's head, after blockr.ui's stylesheet, as the rules that the method of `format()` returns:

```{r}
frontend <- new_blockr_theme(
  light = list("--bk-color-popover" = "#fafafa", "--bk-spacing" = "0.22rem"),
  dark = list("--bk-color-popover" = "#262626", "--bk-spacing" = "0.22rem")
)

cat(format(frontend))
```

Core's method of `frontend_theme()` for `frontend_plugin` returns a theme with no values.
So a frontend that keeps every default needs no method of its own.
Core's basic frontend and the dock keep every default, since their look is blockr.ui's.

A frontend also draws its own parts with the theme variables, as the dock draws its cards, its navbar and the frame around its panels.
So an app's theme restyles them with every other UI.
The frontend's stylesheet takes every colour, face, size, radius and shadow of those parts from a theme variable.
It holds no colour of its own, since the values that the frontend wants its own are in its theme.
A part may need a value that no theme variable gives, such as a grey between two others.
The frontend then takes the variable whose job comes closest, or it derives the value from theme variables in its stylesheet.

No stylesheet of a package but blockr.ui's sets a theme variable, for two reasons:

1. A value that a stylesheet sets on an element below the page's root wins there over the theme of the frontend and over the app's.
2. A value in a stylesheet escapes the frontend's theme, which the frontend's tests read ([Which defaults a frontend keeps](#which-defaults-a-frontend-keeps)).

So the check of the build preset fails a stylesheet of another package that sets a variable under `--bk-`.

### Which value wins

Three sources set the theme variables, each over the one before:

1. The stylesheet of blockr.ui gives every variable its default.
2. The frontend's theme sets the values that the frontend wants its own.
3. The app's theme sets the values that the app wants its own ([An app's theme](#an-apps-theme)).

The order follows from where each source sets its values:

- The stylesheet of blockr.ui sets its defaults inside a cascade layer, Tailwind's `theme`.
  R writes both themes outside any layer, so their values win over the defaults.
- R writes the frontend's theme first and the app's theme after it.
  The rules of the two have the same selectors, so the app's values win over the frontend's.
- Each rule of a theme names `:root` twice beside the mode, as `:root:root[data-bk-mode="light"]`.
  So a theme also wins over a stylesheet that sets a theme variable under `:root[data-bk-mode="light"]`, whichever loads first.

Every element inherits the values from the page's root.
So an overlay takes them too, wherever React Aria puts it on the page.

### Which defaults a frontend keeps

A frontend's tests tell, for each mode, which theme variables the frontend leaves at blockr.ui's defaults.
So a frontend keeps a default only by choice.
The function `unset_variables()` takes a theme and returns, for each mode, the theme variables that the theme sets no value for.
For the theme of the frontend above, `unset_variables()` gives every theme variable but the two that the theme sets:

```{r}
unset <- unset_variables(frontend)

setdiff(theme_variables(), unset$light)
setdiff(theme_variables(), unset$dark)
```

A frontend's tests check that `unset_variables()` returns exactly the defaults that the frontend keeps on purpose.
The test names each of those variables, rather than taking them from `theme_variables()`:

```r
test_that("the frontend keeps the defaults that it means to keep", {
  expect_identical(
    unset_variables(frontend_theme(new_my_frontend())),
    list(
      light = c("--bk-color-background", "--bk-color-foreground", ...),
      dark = c("--bk-color-background", "--bk-color-foreground", ...)
    )
  )
})
```

The test checks each mode on its own.
So a value that the frontend sets for light mode alone shows up in the list for dark mode.

A later version of blockr.ui may add a theme variable, in a minor release.
Then this happens:

1. Every page draws the new variable in blockr.ui's default, so nothing breaks for the users of an app.
2. The frontend's tests fail the next time they run against that version, and they name the new variable.
3. The frontend's author sets the variable in the frontend's theme, or adds it to the defaults that the frontend keeps.

## The components

A module imports the components of blockr.ui from `@blockr/ui`.
They are [React Aria's components](https://react-aria.adobe.com/), drawn with the theme variables after React Aria's Tailwind starter kit.
Each takes React Aria's props and those that the starter kit adds, such as `label`, `description` and `errorMessage`.

| Group | Components |
|---|---|
| Fields | `TextField`, `NumberField`, `SearchField`, `TokenField` with `Token`, `Field`, `Form` and `FormLayout` |
| Picks | `Select` with `SelectItem` and `SelectSection`, `ComboBox` with `ComboBoxItem` and `ComboBoxSection`, `ListBox` with `ListBoxItem`, `Autocomplete` with `useFilter`, `Checkbox`, `CheckboxGroup`, `Radio`, `RadioGroup`, `Switch`, `Slider`, `ToggleButton`, `ToggleButtonGroup`, and `TagGroup` with `Tag` |
| Dates and times | `DateField`, `TimeField`, `DatePicker`, `DateRangePicker`, `Calendar` and `RangeCalendar` |
| Colours | `ColorField`, `ColorPicker`, `ColorArea`, `ColorSlider`, `ColorWheel`, `ColorThumb`, `ColorSwatch`, and `ColorSwatchPicker` with `ColorSwatchPickerItem` |
| Buttons and files | `Button`, `FieldButton`, `DropZone`, `FileTrigger` and `Text` |
| Overlays | `Modal`, `Dialog`, `DialogTrigger`, `AlertDialog`, `Sheet`, `Popover`, `Menu` with `MenuItem`, `MenuSection` and `MenuTrigger`, `SubmenuTrigger`, `CommandPalette`, `Tooltip` with `TooltipTrigger`, `Toast` with `ToastContent`, `ToastQueue` and `ToastRegion`, `Heading`, `Keyboard` and `Focusable` |
| Layout | `Disclosure` with `DisclosureHeader`, `DisclosurePanel` and `DisclosureGroup`, `Tabs` with `TabList`, `Tab` and `TabPanel`, `Toolbar`, `Separator`, `Breadcrumbs` with `Breadcrumb`, `Link`, `Meter` and `ProgressBar` |
| Collections | `Table` with `TableHeader`, `TableBody`, `Column`, `Row` and `Cell`, `Tree` with `TreeItem`, `NavigationTree` with `NavigationTreeHeader`, `NavigationTreeSection`, `NavigationTreeItem`, `NavigationTreeItemContent` and `NavigationTreeItemLink`, `GridList` with `GridListHeader`, `GridListSection` and `GridListItem`, and `useDragAndDrop` with `DropIndicator` |
| Icons | `Icon` and `iconMarkup()` ([The icons](#the-icons)) |

A component draws with the theme variables alone, never with a colour of Tailwind's palette.
It opens its overlays in React Aria's portal, at the end of the page's body.
The overlays stack at the layer that `--bk-z-index-overlay` gives.
A component knows no block, no host and no board option.
An input takes its value through its prop `bound` instead ([How an input takes its value](#how-an-input-takes-its-value)).

The component `FormLayout` lays out the controls of a UI one below the other.
It only arranges them, so a block's UI uses it without a form.
The component `Form` is React Aria's form element, with its validation.

Say a block keeps the first or the last rows of its data.
Its state holds how many rows, `n`, and from which end, `direction`.
Its UI might draw these controls:

```tsx
import type { ReactElement } from "react";
import { FormLayout, NumberField, ToggleButton, ToggleButtonGroup } from "@blockr/ui";
import type { Bound } from "@blockr/ui";

export function HeadControls({ n, direction }: { n: Bound; direction: Bound }): ReactElement {
  return (
    <FormLayout>
      <NumberField bound={n} label="Number of rows" minValue={0} step={1} />
      <ToggleButtonGroup bound={direction} label="Direction" disallowEmptySelection>
        <ToggleButton id="head">Head</ToggleButton>
        <ToggleButton id="tail">Tail</ToggleButton>
      </ToggleButtonGroup>
    </FormLayout>
  );
}
```

The block's UI binds the controls to its state with the hooks of core's React SDK (`vignette("create-block", package = "blockr.core")`):

```tsx
import type { ReactElement } from "react";
import type { BlockHost } from "@blockr/core";
import { reactModule, useValue } from "@blockr/core/react";
import type { ModuleProps } from "@blockr/core/react";
import { HeadControls } from "./head-controls.tsx";

type State = { n: number; direction: "head" | "tail" };

export const api = 1;

function HeadBlock({ host }: ModuleProps<BlockHost<State>>): ReactElement {
  return <HeadControls n={useValue(host, "n")} direction={useValue(host, "direction")} />;
}

export default reactModule(HeadBlock);
```

Beside its components, blockr.ui puts the whole of React Aria on the page, once.
A module imports React Aria's other components from `react-aria-components`.
It imports React Aria's hooks from `react-aria`, and the state that the hooks keep from `react-stately`.
A module uses them for what no component of blockr.ui does, such as a table that draws thousands of cells without hooks in each.
A module still draws with blockr.ui's component wherever blockr.ui has one.

A module never imports a package under `@react-aria/` or `@react-stately/`, nor an entry point inside React Aria's packages, such as `react-aria-components/Table`.
Each of them would bundle a second copy of React Aria, with React contexts of its own.
An item of the second copy inside blockr.ui's `ComboBox`, for one, would find no combo box.
So the build preset fails such an import ([The React half](#the-react-half)).

### The icons

The icons of blockr's UIs are [Lucide's](https://lucide.dev/icons/), stroked lines with round caps.
The entry `@blockr/ui/icons` offers every icon of Lucide's package `lucide`, at the version that blockr.ui pins.
Each icon keeps the name that `lucide` exports, such as `Pin` or `Trash`.
Each is the icon's shape as data, which the component `Icon` draws:

```tsx
import type { ReactElement } from "react";
import { Button, Icon } from "@blockr/ui";
import { Pin } from "@blockr/ui/icons";

export function PinButton({ onPress }: { onPress: () => void }): ReactElement {
  return (
    <Button variant="quiet" aria-label="Pin the panel" onPress={onPress}>
      <Icon icon={Pin} />
    </Button>
  );
}
```

The component draws the shape in the colour of the text around it.
It draws it 14 pixels wide, unless it is given a `size`.
It hides the icon from screen readers unless it is given a `label`.
What holds an icon names what it does instead, as the button's `aria-label` does above.

The function `iconMarkup()` writes the same drawing as SVG markup, which is what the icon of a board action is:

```ts
import { iconMarkup } from "@blockr/ui";
import { Plus } from "@blockr/ui/icons";

export const icon = iconMarkup(Plus);
```

The page's import map names no entry for `@blockr/ui/icons`.
So the build preset bundles the icons that a package imports into the package's own build.
The page then loads only the icons that its packages draw.
A package draws a new icon without a change to blockr.ui, unless Lucide added the icon after the version that blockr.ui pins.
Where Lucide renames an icon, it keeps the old name as an alias, so an import of the old name still builds.
A module never imports one of Lucide's packages itself, such as `lucide` or `lucide-react`.
The build preset fails a build that does.

### How an input takes its value

An input of blockr.ui takes the value that it shows and submits through its prop `bound`, an object of the interface `Bound`:

```ts
export interface Bound {
  readonly value: Json | undefined;          // the value that the binding last gave the input to show
  readonly error: string | null;             // why the last submit was refused, which the input shows below itself
  get(): Json | undefined;                   // the value as it is held now
  commit(value: Json): Promise<boolean>;     // submits a pick at once, and resolves with whether it was taken
  unset(): Promise<boolean>;                 // clears the value, as for an arg without a default
  type(value: Json | undefined): void;       // takes what the user typed, which is submitted once the user pauses
  flush(): void;                             // submits what the user typed at once, as on Enter or as the user leaves the input
}
```

The interface names no host, no block and no board option.
A block's UI gets a `Bound` from core's `useValue()`, which binds a state arg of the block or the value of a board option.
Whatever implements `Bound` keeps the rules of a binding, as core's binding does:

1. The binding holds a value, and gives it to the input as `value`.
2. The input calls `commit()` as the user picks, `type()` as the user types, and `flush()` as the user presses Enter or leaves the input.
3. The binding waits for the user to pause before it submits what the user typed.
4. While the user types, the binding gives the input no value that the host announces.
5. Where the host refuses a submit, the binding gives the input the reason, as `error`, and the input shows it below itself.

So every input keeps the same rules, whoever implements `Bound`.
A number passes through wrong values as the user types, as 15 on the way to 150.
So a number field never calls `type()`, and a pause submits nothing.
It calls `commit()` as the user presses Enter, leaves the field or steps the number.

An input without a `bound` takes React Aria's value props instead: `value` with `onChange`, or `defaultValue`.
A search field whose text no host holds is one such input.

### Testing what a package draws

The entry `@blockr/ui/stubs` holds the tools with which a package's tests act on blockr.ui's components.
Its function `stubBound()` makes a stub of `Bound`.
The stub holds a value and records each value that an input commits, types and flushes.
It refuses every submit with an error once a test asks it to.
A component that a test draws binds an input to the stub through `useStubBound()`, as a block's UI binds one through core's `useValue()`.
So a package tests its controls apart from any host:

```tsx
import type { ReactElement } from "react";
import { expect, test } from "vitest";
import { draw, labelled, press, step, stubBound, texts, toggleButton, type, useStubBound } from "@blockr/ui/stubs";
import { HeadControls } from "./head-controls.tsx";

test("submits the number as the user presses Enter, and the end as the user picks it", async () => {
  const n = stubBound(6);
  const direction = stubBound("head");
  function Controls(): ReactElement {
    return <HeadControls n={useStubBound(n)} direction={useStubBound(direction)} />;
  }
  const { el } = draw(<Controls />);
  const field = labelled(el, "Number of rows");
  expect(field.value).toBe("6");

  await step(() => {
    type(field, "10");
  });
  expect(n.committed).toEqual([]);
  await step(() => {
    press(field, "Enter");
  });
  expect(n.value).toBe(10);

  await step(() => {
    toggleButton(el, "Direction", "Tail").click();
  });
  expect(direction.committed).toEqual(["tail"]);

  n.refuse("The table has 8 rows.");
  await step(() => {
    type(field, "20");
    press(field, "Enter");
  });
  expect(n.value).toBe(10);
  expect(texts(el, '[role="alert"]')).toEqual(["The table has 8 rows."]);
});
```

The test draws the controls with `draw()` and acts on them as a user does:

- The helper `type()` types into a field one keystroke at a time.
- The helper `press()` presses a key.
- The helper `toggleButton()` finds a toggle button by the label of its group and by its own.

Each act runs in `step()`, which lets React draw what the act changed before the test reads the page.
Other helpers pick the rows of a select, as `picked()` does.
Others open a menu, or list the rows of a table, a tree or a grid list.
They know where React Aria draws each part, such as a select's list at the end of the page's body.
A change to a component and the change to its helpers ship in the same release of blockr.ui.

The stub itself is no `Bound`, so TypeScript refuses to let an input take the stub directly.
Such an input would never draw again as the stub's value changes.
The stub takes every submit at once, with no pause.
A test of a binding's own rules, such as the pause before a submit, binds the input through `useValue()` on core's stubs of the hosts.

The tests run on Vitest, with happy-dom as their DOM.
Loading `@blockr/ui/stubs` makes happy-dom do as a browser does where blockr.ui's components need it.

### Failing a test on what it prints

Vitest shows what a passing test prints to the console only on request.
So an error or a warning that a passing test sets off goes unseen.
The setup `@blockr/ui/stubs/setup` fails a test on any error or warning that it prints, through `console.error()` or `console.warn()`.
The messages include React's warning of an update outside `act()`.
The helpers `step()` and `draw()` run inside `act()`, so a test that acts and draws through them sets off no such warning.
A package lists the setup in the `setupFiles` of its `vitest.config.ts`, before its own setup files:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from "vitest/config";

export default defineConfig({
  test: {
    environment: "happy-dom",
    include: ["srcts/**/*.test.{ts,tsx}"],
    setupFiles: ["@blockr/ui/stubs/setup", "./srcts/testing/setup.ts"],
  },
});
```

The setup checks each test after the test's own hooks have run, so a message that a hook prints fails the test too.
A message printed outside any test, such as one that a test file prints as it loads, fails the file once its tests have run.
Every message still reaches the console, so Vitest shows it with the test that fails.

A test that sets off an error on purpose names it with `expectedErrors()`, which takes the errors that match its patterns off the console for the rest of the test.
It gives the messages that it took, in order, so that the test can count them:

```ts
import { expect, test } from "vitest";
import { expectedErrors } from "@blockr/ui/stubs";
import { loadTable } from "./table.ts";

test("logs the error of a request that fails, and shows no rows", async () => {
  const taken = expectedErrors(/HTTP 503/);

  const rows = await loadTable("https://example.org/unavailable");

  expect(rows).toEqual([]);
  expect(taken).toHaveLength(1);
});
```

A package may set off an error that it cannot fix yet, such as an error that another package fixes in a later release.
The package holds such an exception in a setup file of its own, with `allowMessage()`.
The check given to `allowMessage()` runs as the message is printed, so it can read from the stack where the message came from:

```ts
import { allowMessage } from "@blockr/ui/stubs/setup";

// React's error that drawForm() of another package calls flushSync() while
// React draws, until that package fixes it.
allowMessage(
  (message) =>
    message.startsWith("flushSync was called from inside a lifecycle method") &&
    /\bdrawForm\b/.test(new Error().stack ?? ""),
);
```

The check of `allowMessage()` and the patterns of `expectedErrors()` read a message as the console prints it, with the values of placeholders such as `%s` filled in.

The setup also gives happy-dom the element `search`, which browsers draw as a plain element, but which happy-dom does not know.
Without it, React would warn of an unknown element wherever a UI draws a `search`, and the setup would fail the test.

## Building on blockr.ui

A package builds its modules and its stylesheet against blockr.ui through the build preset, `@blockr/ui/build`.
The preset has two halves.
The package's call of esbuild takes the half for React, and the package's stylesheet imports the half for Tailwind CSS.
Core's `install_js_types()` puts `@blockr/ui` into a package's `node_modules`, beside `@blockr/core`, where the package depends on blockr.ui directly or through core.

### The React half

A package's build spreads the options of the preset into its own call of esbuild:

```ts
import * as esbuild from "esbuild";
import { preset } from "@blockr/ui/build";

await esbuild.build({ ...preset, entryPoints: ["srcts/controls.tsx"], outdir: "inst/js" });
```

The preset bundles a module as an ES module for the browser.
It leaves these imports to the page's import map:

- React's entry points: `react`, `react/jsx-runtime`, `react-dom` and `react-dom/client`.
- The components, `@blockr/ui`.
- React Aria's three packages: `react-aria-components`, `react-aria` and `react-stately`.

So the files of a package hold none of them.
The page runs one copy of each, from blockr.ui's files.
Say `srcts/controls.tsx` exports the controls and the button of the examples above.
The build writes it into a file that starts with these lines:

```js
// srcts/head-controls.tsx
import { FormLayout, NumberField, ToggleButton, ToggleButtonGroup } from "@blockr/ui";
import { jsx, jsxs } from "react/jsx-runtime";
```

The preset bundles the icons that a module imports from `@blockr/ui/icons`, since the page's import map names no entry for them.
The preset fails a build that would bundle a second copy of something that the page holds once.
Its error names what to import instead.
It fails a build that imports any of these:

- An entry point of React that the import map does not name, such as `react-dom/server`.
- A package under `@react-aria/` or `@react-stately/`, or an entry point inside React Aria's packages, such as `react-aria-components/Table`.
- One of React Aria's packages at another version than the one in blockr.ui's files.
- One of Lucide's packages, such as `lucide` or `lucide-react`.

A package that builds on core spreads core's preset, `@blockr/core/build`, in place of blockr.ui's.
Core's preset extends blockr.ui's with core's own entries, such as `@blockr/core/react`.

Beside the preset, `@blockr/ui/build` holds two more parts of every package's build, whichever preset the package spreads:

- The vendor check, `vendorCheck`, is a plugin of esbuild.
  It fails a build that puts code from `node_modules` into one of the package's own files.
  A package's own files hold its own code alone, unminified.
  The libraries that it bundles, such as the icons that it draws, go minified into a vendor file of its own.
  Its own files import them from there.
- The function `staticImports()` lists what each file of a build imports up front.
  The package writes that list into `inst/js/preload.json`.
  R names those files in the head of the page, so that the browser fetches them as the page loads.

### The Tailwind half

A package that writes classes builds them with Tailwind CSS, under a prefix of its own ([Prefixes](#prefixes)).
Its stylesheet imports Tailwind's theme and utilities under that prefix, and then the stylesheet of the preset, as core's stylesheet does under `bc`:

```css
@layer theme;
@import "tailwindcss/theme.css" layer(theme) prefix(bc);
@import "tailwindcss/utilities.css" source(none);
@import "@blockr/ui/preset.css";
@source "./**/*.{ts,tsx}";
```

The stylesheet of the preset maps each name of Tailwind's theme that has a theme variable onto that variable.
So the package's classes compile to reads of the theme variables.
Take a count of rows in a muted pill, written with core's prefix:

```tsx
<p className="bc:m-0 bc:rounded-md bc:bg-muted bc:px-2 bc:text-sm bc:text-muted-foreground">{rows} rows</p>
```

For it, Tailwind writes these rules:

```css
.bc\:m-0 {
  margin: 0;
}

.bc\:rounded-md {
  border-radius: calc(var(--bk-radius) * .8);
}

.bc\:bg-muted {
  background-color: var(--bk-color-muted);
}

.bc\:px-2 {
  padding-inline: calc(var(--bk-spacing) * 2);
}

.bc\:text-sm {
  font-size: var(--bk-text-sm);
  line-height: var(--tw-leading, calc(1.25 / .875));
}

.bc\:text-muted-foreground {
  color: var(--bk-color-muted-foreground);
}
```

The stylesheet of the preset does four more things:

- It drops Tailwind's palette, but for black and white.
  It also drops the steps of the faces, the sizes of text, the radii and the shadows that the theme variables lack.
  Tailwind writes nothing for a class that it does not know, without a warning.
  So the check fails such a class ([The checks](#the-checks)).
- It keys the variant `dark:` on `data-bk-mode="dark"` on the page's root.
- It leaves out Tailwind's reset of the whole page, so that nothing that one package loads styles the elements of another.
- It keeps the utilities outside any cascade layer, so that other CSS on the page, such as Bootstrap's, does not win over them.

### Prefixes

Tailwind writes CSS only for the classes that it finds in the files that it scans.
So each package builds its own classes, under a prefix of its own, as core writes `bc:flex`.
Two stylesheets built apart that wrote the same class would override each other in the order in which they load.

The prefix `bk` belongs to blockr.ui.
Its theme variables, its classes and the mode attribute `data-bk-mode` carry it.
The classes under `bk:` come and go with blockr.ui's components.
So no other package writes a class under `bk:`, and the check fails another package's build that does.
A package that writes no classes, such as one whose CSS is written by hand, runs no Tailwind.
It reads the theme variables in its CSS, as `var(--bk-color-card)`, and runs the check on its CSS and on its code.

### The list of theme variables

What the stylesheet of blockr.ui provides other packages is a list, which blockr.ui declares.
It holds the names of the theme variables, the font Open Sans and the mode attribute.
The build preset exports the list as `themeVariables`.
In R, `theme_variables()` returns the names of the theme variables, from a file that blockr.ui's build writes from the same list.
So the two never disagree.
The stylesheet of blockr.ui sets every variable of the list, whether or not one of its own components reads it.
So another package never loses a variable that it reads.
The classes of blockr.ui are not on the list.

The list is a promise to other packages:

- A minor release of blockr.ui may add to the list.
- Only a major release removes or renames what the list holds.
- Each major release names one version of Tailwind CSS, which every package's build runs.
  The stylesheets of all packages register Tailwind's own properties, such as `--tw-shadow`, without a prefix.
  Stylesheets written by two versions of Tailwind could register them differently.

### The checks

The function `themeCheck()` of `@blockr/ui/build` checks the stylesheets that a build wrote and the code that it wrote them from.
It fails the build in these cases:

- A stylesheet reads a variable under `--bk-` that the list lacks, in plain CSS or in an arbitrary value.
- A stylesheet sets a variable under `--bk-`, which only blockr.ui's stylesheet may do.
- Another version of Tailwind CSS than blockr.ui's wrote a stylesheet.
- The code names a colour of Tailwind's palette, or a step that the theme variables lack, under any prefix.
- The code names a class under `bk:`.

A package's build compiles its stylesheet with Tailwind's plugin for PostCSS, as core's and blockr.ui's builds do.
It then runs the check on the stylesheet and on the files that Tailwind scanned for classes:

```ts
import { readFile, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import tailwindcss from "@tailwindcss/postcss";
import * as esbuild from "esbuild";
import postcss from "postcss";
import { preset, themeCheck } from "@blockr/ui/build";

await esbuild.build({ ...preset, entryPoints: ["srcts/controls.tsx"], outdir: "inst/js" });

const from = "srcts/index.css";
const result = await postcss([tailwindcss({ optimize: { minify: false } })]).process(await readFile(from, "utf8"), { from });
await writeFile("inst/js/controls.css", result.css);

// Tailwind tells PostCSS of each file that it scanned for classes, as a dependency of the stylesheet.
const scanned = result.messages.flatMap((message) =>
  message.type === "dependency" && typeof message.file === "string" && !message.file.endsWith(".css") ? [message.file] : [],
);

await themeCheck({ stylesheets: ["inst/js/controls.css"], code: scanned });
```

For a stylesheet and a file of code that break the check, the error names each problem by its file and line:

```
The build fails themeCheck() of @blockr/ui/build:
bad.css:1: The stylesheet reads --bk-color-blue, which the list of theme variables lacks. Read one of the variables that themeVariables in @blockr/ui/build lists.
bad.css:2: The stylesheet sets --bk-color-card, but only blockr.ui's stylesheet sets variables under --bk-. A frontend gives its values in a theme, which its method of frontend_theme() returns in R.
srcts/bad.tsx:1: bc:bg-blue-600 names blue-600 of Tailwind's palette, which the build preset drops, so the class writes nothing. Draw with the colour of a job, such as primary or muted-foreground, which a theme and the mode reach.
srcts/bad.tsx:1: bk:flex is a class under bk:, which blockr.ui alone writes, for its own components. Write it under the package's own prefix.
srcts/bad.tsx:1: bc:shadow-2xl names a step of the shadows that the theme variables lack, which the build preset drops, so the class writes nothing. Draw with a step that they hold: shadow-sm, shadow-md, shadow-lg or shadow-none.
```

## An app's theme

An app may give the page a theme of its own, whose values win over the frontend's and over blockr.ui's defaults.
So a company's design restyles the whole page, under any frontend, the frontend's own parts included.
The app's theme sets theme variables, as a frontend's theme does, so one theme fits every frontend.
It sets the variables whose values the app wants its own, and leaves the rest to the frontend.

The theme variables name jobs, so an app's theme sets every job whose look it changes.
A company's brand colour, for one, takes four variables in each mode:

- The variable `--bk-color-primary` takes the colour itself.
- The variable `--bk-color-primary-foreground` takes the text on it.
- The variable `--bk-color-primary-text` takes the text of links and messages.
- The variable `--bk-color-ring` takes the focus ring.

Nothing derives the values of other jobs from the brand colour as the page draws.
So a theme holds every value that the page draws, where its author sees and checks it.
A package that makes themes, such as blockr.theme, may compute such values as it makes a theme.

The function `new_blockr_theme()` makes the theme, from values for theme variables and the files of any fonts that the theme brings:

```{r}
theme <- new_blockr_theme(
  light = list(
    "--bk-color-primary" = "#be2bbb",
    "--bk-color-primary-foreground" = "#ffffff",
    "--bk-color-primary-text" = "#9b1f98",
    "--bk-color-ring" = "#be2bbb",
    "--bk-font-sans" = "Inter, sans-serif"
  ),
  dark = list(
    "--bk-color-primary" = "#d66bd3",
    "--bk-color-primary-foreground" = "#0e1219",
    "--bk-color-primary-text" = "#e08fdd",
    "--bk-color-ring" = "#d66bd3",
    "--bk-font-sans" = "Inter, sans-serif"
  ),
  fonts = list(
    list(family = "Inter", file = "fonts/inter-latin.woff2", weight = "100 900")
  )
)

is_blockr_theme(theme)
```

The theme's `light` and `dark` hold the values of each mode, each under the full name of its theme variable.
Each value holds in its own mode alone.
So a theme with values for light mode alone leaves dark mode to the frontend.
A value is any CSS value, which R writes into the page as it is.
Its `fonts` hold a face for each file of a font, with the font's `family`, the path of its `file`, and the `weight` and the `style` of the face.
The weight and the style default to `normal`, as they do for a face in CSS.

The function refuses a name that `theme_variables()` lacks, and names it:

```{r, error = TRUE}
new_blockr_theme(light = list("--bk-color-primay" = "#be2bbb"))
```

So a misspelt name, or a name that a later version of blockr.ui drops, stops the app as it starts.
The function also refuses a value that holds `}` or `<`, either of which would end the rule or the element that holds it.

An app gives its theme to core's `serve()`, whose argument `theme` defaults to the blockr option `theme`:

```r
library(blockr.core)

serve(new_board(), theme = theme)
```

An app's script may set the R option `blockr.theme` instead, as `options(blockr.theme = theme)` does.
A site-wide R profile, `Rprofile.site`, can set the option too, for every app that runs on its installation of R.
An app's script overrides it.
The theme is an R object, so no environment variable can give it.
The function `serve()` refuses a theme that `new_blockr_theme()` did not make, such as a string.
Where nothing sets it, the page draws with the frontend's values and blockr.ui's defaults.
Each method of `serve()` takes the theme, so a block that `serve()` serves alone draws in it too.

Core writes the theme's rules into the page's head, after the frontend's, with the method of `format()`:

```{r}
cat(format(theme))
```

So the theme holds from the first paint.
Every board that the app opens draws in it, since the page keeps its head.
As `dark_mode` switches `data-bk-mode`, the browser applies the rule of the new mode.
For each font of the theme, core serves the font's file and writes a face for it, with `@font-face` and `font-display: swap`.
It names the file in the page's head as well, so that the browser fetches it as the page loads.
Until the file arrives, the text draws in the next face of the stack.

A theme sets values, never parts.
So a company's logo is the frontend's to take, through an argument or a blockr option of the frontend's own.
A theme holds for the whole page, since its rules set the page's root, from which every overlay inherits.
The colours of the categories of block classes stay outside every theme.
Core's blockr option `category_colors` sets them.
